headline: Chancellor John Healey delivers his first Budget today with little room for manoeuvre

terms.meaning: The government's yearly statement of how much it will tax and spend.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, an independent body that forecasts the public finances.
Bonds the UK government sells to borrow money.

levels.headline: Chancellor John Healey delivers his first Budget today with little room for manoeuvre
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey presents his first Budget to Parliament today, 28 October 2026, the first under Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its forecasts alongside it.
Healey has said the government will keep to its fiscal rules and hold a buffer against uncertainty. Commentary suggests that buffer may shrink to cover the cost of the Iran war and higher defence spending, though tax rises still look likely. Bank taxes have been mentioned as a possibility, and an extension of fuel duty relief could cost more than £2 billion.
Pressure comes from the gilt market: UK government borrowing costs are the highest in the G7 and public sector net debt has passed £3 trillion. Separately, the Prime Minister has said a further £432 million for rough sleeping will be confirmed in the Budget.
levels.why: The Budget sets taxes and spending, and the bond market's reaction will affect borrowing costs for everyone.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget arrives under pressure from bond markets and a tighter fiscal position
levels.body:
John Healey delivers his first Budget today, Wednesday 28 October, with the OBR forecast published at the same time. It is the first Budget of Andy Burnham's government.
Healey has promised to stay within the fiscal rules and keep a buffer against shocks. A CNBC opinion piece expects that buffer to absorb much of the pressure from the Iran war and defence costs, but says tax increases remain likely, possibly including a tax change aimed at banks. Extending fuel duty relief could cost over £2 billion.
Investors in gilts want restraint. UK borrowing costs are the highest in the G7, and public sector net debt has topped £3 trillion. The Prime Minister has also said £432 million more for tackling rough sleeping will be confirmed.
levels.why: Decisions made today could change taxes, public services and the cost of mortgages.

levels.headline: Healey sets out his first Budget with markets watching closely
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey stands up in Parliament today to deliver his first Budget. It is also the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and independent forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility come out at the same time.
He has said he will follow the government's own borrowing rules and keep some spare room in case things go wrong. That spare room may now be smaller because the war with Iran and higher defence spending have raised costs. Taxes are still expected to rise in some areas, and banks could be targeted. Keeping fuel duty relief could cost over £2 billion.
Investors who lend to the government are nervous. Its borrowing costs are the highest in the G7, and national debt has passed £3 trillion.
levels.why: It shows how the government plans to pay for public services and how far it will ask people and firms to pay more.

levels.headline: The Chancellor gives his first Budget today as the government faces high borrowing costs
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey gives his first Budget today. This is the government's yearly plan for taxes and spending. Prime Minister Andy Burnham leads the government, and an independent watchdog called the OBR will publish its forecasts at the same time.
Healey says he will stick to the government's rules on borrowing and keep a cushion in case of bad news. Writers who follow the markets think that cushion may get smaller, because the Iran war and extra defence spending cost money. They still expect some tax rises, perhaps on banks. Keeping the cut in fuel duty could cost more than £2 billion.
The government borrows by selling bonds, called gilts. The rates it pays are the highest in the G7, and national debt is above £3 trillion.
levels.why: Your taxes, public services and loan costs can all be affected by what is announced.

levels.headline: Today the Chancellor announces how the government will raise and spend money
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey is giving the Budget today. A Budget is when the government says how much tax it will collect and what it will spend the money on. It is his first one, and Andy Burnham is Prime Minister. A group of independent experts, the OBR, shares its own predictions at the same time.
Healey says the government will follow its own rules about borrowing. He wants to keep a small safety cushion in case something goes wrong. The war with Iran and higher spending on defence have used up some of that cushion. Many people expect a few taxes to go up, maybe for banks.
The government borrows by selling bonds. It now pays more for this than any other G7 country, and its debt is over £3 trillion.
levels.why: The Budget affects what people pay in tax and how much money goes to schools, hospitals and housing.

levels.headline: The Chancellor sets out the government's plan for money today
levels.body:
Today the Chancellor, John Healey, gives the Budget. The Budget is the government's plan for the year. It says what taxes people and companies will pay, and what the government will spend. It is his first one. Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister. Independent experts at the OBR will share their own money forecasts too.
Healey says the government will keep to its borrowing rules. He also wants a small cushion of spare money. But the war with Iran and more spending on the army have made that cushion smaller. Some taxes may go up, perhaps for banks.
The government borrows money by selling bonds. It pays more to do this than any other G7 country. Its total debt is over £3 trillion. The Prime Minister also says £432 million more will go to help people who sleep on the streets.
levels.why: It decides how much tax people pay and which services get money.

levels.headline: Today is Budget day: the government says how it will use money
levels.body:
Today is Budget day in the UK. The Chancellor, John Healey, will tell Parliament how the government plans to raise money and spend it. The Prime Minister is Andy Burnham. Parliament is where MPs meet to make laws and decide big things.
The government has rules about how much it can borrow. Healey says he will follow them. He also wants to keep some spare money in case of a nasty surprise. Costs have gone up because of the war with Iran and more spending on defence, so the spare money may shrink. Some taxes might rise, perhaps for banks.
The government borrows by selling bonds. Lenders now want a high price for lending to it. The government's debt is more than £3 trillion. The Prime Minister also plans £432 million more to help people sleeping rough.
levels.why: It can change the taxes your family pays and the money spent on things like hospitals and schools.

levels.headline: The government shares its plan for money today
levels.body:
Today the Chancellor, John Healey, tells the country how the government will get and spend money. This is called the Budget. It is his first one. The Prime Minister is Andy Burnham.
Think of a family planning its money for the year. The government does the same, but with much bigger sums. It collects tax from people and companies. Then it spends the money on schools, hospitals and roads. Healey says the government will follow its own rules on borrowing. He wants to keep a little spare money for emergencies. But a war with Iran and more spending on the army have made that spare money smaller. Some taxes may go up, maybe for banks.
The government also borrows. It now pays more to borrow than other rich countries. Its debt is over £3 trillion.
levels.why: It decides how much tax people pay and what the government can afford to do.

levels.headline: A big money plan for the country is shared today
levels.body:
Today a man called John Healey shares a big plan about money for the whole country. He is the Chancellor. That is the person in charge of the government's money. The plan is called the Budget.
Imagine your class has a pot of pocket money. Each week, everyone puts a little in. Then the class chooses what to buy with it. The country works like that. People pay tax, and the government spends it on things like schools and hospitals. This year things cost more. There is a war far away, and soldiers need more equipment too. So the pot is under pressure. Some people may have to pay a bit more tax.
The government also borrows, like asking to borrow a friend's money. Now lenders ask for more back.
levels.why: The plan decides how much money goes to schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: Think of the country as a big family deciding how to share out money
levels.body:
Today the person in charge of the country's money, John Healey, tells everyone his plan. It is called the Budget. Imagine a school fair where everyone pays a little to join in, and the teachers then choose what to buy with the money. That is a bit like how a country works.
The country gets its money from tax. Tax is a small part of what people earn or spend, handed over to pay for shared things such as hospitals and schools. This year things cost more. There is a war far away, and the army needs more too. So the money is stretched thin. Some people might be asked to pay a little more tax.
The country has also borrowed, like borrowing from a friend. Now the friends want more back.
levels.why: It helps decide how much money goes to the things we all share, like schools.

headline: S&P 500 closes up 0.6% at about 7,722.6 as chip stocks lead Wall Street higher

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies.
An index dominated by technology companies.
Computer chips, the tiny parts inside nearly all electronics.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes up 0.6% at about 7,722.6 as chip stocks lead Wall Street higher
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed up about 0.6% at around 7,722.60 on Tuesday 27 October, its second straight gain. Trading Economics put the close at 7,723.35, up 0.61%; the small gap reflects different quote times.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up about 16 points, or 0.03%, to about 52,377.57. The Nasdaq Composite was the strongest of the three, rising about 1.18% to around 26,477.81, led by a rally in semiconductor shares.
A slide in oil prices also helped sentiment. The Federal Reserve began a two-day policy meeting on the day, and a CNBC survey found economists expect rate rises later but not this week. Wednesday's session was still to come when these figures were compiled.
levels.why: US share prices influence pensions, investments and global markets, and the Fed's next move matters for borrowing costs.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends higher as chipmakers drive the Nasdaq up more than 1%
levels.body:
US stocks closed higher on Tuesday 27 October, the last completed session. The S&P 500 rose about 0.6% to around 7,722.60, its second straight daily gain, according to CNBC. Trading Economics gave 7,723.35, up 0.61%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average added only about 16 points, or 0.03%, to about 52,377.57. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed about 1.18% to around 26,477.81 as chip stocks rallied.
Falling oil prices supported the mood. The Federal Reserve started a two-day meeting, and a CNBC survey suggests economists expect interest rate rises, but not at this meeting.
levels.why: It shows how investors are feeling before an important Federal Reserve decision.

levels.headline: US shares rise, helped by technology and cheaper oil
levels.body:
The main US share indexes all closed higher on Tuesday 27 October, the most recent full day of trading. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, rose about 0.6% to around 7,722.60. That was its second rise in a row.
The Dow Jones index, which follows 30 large firms, barely moved. It gained about 16 points, or 0.03%, to about 52,377.57. The Nasdaq Composite, full of technology companies, did best. It rose about 1.18% to around 26,477.81 as makers of computer chips did well.
Oil prices fell, which also helped. The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, began a two-day meeting. Economists in a survey expect it to raise interest rates later, but not this week.
levels.why: Share prices affect savings, pensions and how confident businesses feel.

levels.headline: US shares edge higher as chip stocks lift the Nasdaq
levels.body:
US shares ended higher on Tuesday 27 October, the last completed session. The S&P 500 gained about 0.6% to close near 7,722.60, a second daily rise. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was almost flat, up about 16 points or 0.03% at 52,377.57, while the Nasdaq Composite jumped about 1.18% to 26,477.81.
Chipmakers led the rally, and a fall in oil prices added to the cheerful mood. Investors were also looking ahead to the Federal Reserve, which began a two-day meeting. A CNBC survey of economists found they expect the Fed to raise interest rates later this year, but not at this meeting.
Wednesday's session had not finished when these figures were compiled.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and savings, and they show how confident investors feel.

levels.headline: US stocks climb as chip companies lead the way
levels.body:
American shares went up on Tuesday 27 October, the latest day when the market had closed. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 large US firms, rose about 0.6% to around 7,722.60. It was the second day in a row that it went up.
The Dow Jones, which tracks 30 big companies, hardly changed. It rose about 16 points, or 0.03%, to about 52,377.57. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, rose most. It went up about 1.18% to around 26,477.81. Companies that make computer chips did especially well.
Oil also got cheaper, which helped. The US central bank, called the Fed, began a two-day meeting. Experts expect it to raise interest rates later, but not right now.
levels.why: Rising share prices can mean more confidence, but they can change quickly.

levels.headline: American share prices went up on Tuesday
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States rose on Tuesday 27 October. That was the last full day of trading. A share is a small piece of a company. The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big American companies, and together their prices rose about 0.6%. The number ended at around 7,722.60.
Another list, the Dow Jones, follows 30 big firms. It barely moved. It rose about 16 points, or 0.03%, to about 52,377.57. A third list, the Nasdaq, has lots of technology firms. It rose about 1.18% to around 26,477.81. Firms that make computer chips did well.
The price of oil fell as well. The US bank that sets interest rates started a meeting. Experts think it will raise rates later.
levels.why: Share prices show how confident people are about the economy.

levels.headline: US share prices rose, led by computer chip firms
levels.body:
Share prices in America went up on Tuesday 27 October. That was the last full day of trading. A share is a small slice of a company that people can buy. The S&P 500 follows 500 big American firms, and it rose about 0.6% to around 7,722.60. It also rose the day before.
The Dow Jones follows 30 big firms. It hardly moved, rising about 16 points to about 52,377.57. The Nasdaq has many technology firms. It rose most, by about 1.18%, to around 26,477.81. Companies that make computer chips did best.
Oil got cheaper too. America's central bank, which sets interest rates, began a two-day meeting. Experts think it will raise rates later, but not yet.
levels.why: Share prices can affect pensions and show how people feel about the economy.

levels.headline: Share prices in America went up on Tuesday
levels.body:
On Tuesday 27 October, share prices in America went up. Tuesday was the last full day when the stock market was open. A share is a tiny piece of a company. When many people want to buy shares, prices rise.
There are lists that show how shares are doing. The S&P 500 follows 500 big firms. It went up about 0.6% to around 7,722.60. The Dow Jones follows 30 big firms. It hardly changed. It went up about 0.03% to about 52,377.57. The Nasdaq follows many technology firms. It went up about 1.18% to around 26,477.81. Firms that make computer chips did best.
Oil got cheaper, too. America's central bank is meeting this week. It decides how dear it is to borrow money.
levels.why: Share prices tell us how people feel about companies and the economy.

levels.headline: Money markets in America had a happy day on Tuesday
levels.body:
On Tuesday, lots of shares in America went up in price. Shares are tiny pieces of companies that people buy and sell. Imagine a swap market at school where stickers are traded. When many children want a sticker, its price goes up. Shares work in a similar way.
The list of 500 big firms, called the S&P 500, went up a bit, by about 0.6%. A list of 30 big firms, the Dow Jones, hardly moved. A list of tech firms, the Nasdaq, rose the most, by about 1.18%. Firms that make computer chips did best. Computer chips are tiny parts inside phones and games.
Oil also got cheaper. The bank that decides how dear borrowing is has a meeting this week.
levels.why: It shows how people feel about money and companies.

levels.headline: On Tuesday, the price of many American companies went up a little
levels.body:
On Tuesday, lots of company shares in America cost a bit more. A share is a tiny piece of a company, like owning one slice of a very big cake. When lots of people want slices, the price of each slice goes up.
There are scoreboards for shares. One scoreboard follows 500 big firms. It went up about 0.6%. Another follows 30 firms and hardly moved. A third follows technology firms and went up the most, about 1.18%. The firms that make computer chips did best. Chips are the tiny brains inside phones and games.
Oil, which makes cars go, also got cheaper. The big bank that decides how costly it is to borrow money has a meeting this week.
levels.why: It tells us if people feel hopeful about companies and money.

headline: Markets price in a Bank of England rate rise to 4% on 5 November after inflation hits 3.5%

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences loan and savings rates.
The Monetary Policy Committee, which votes on interest rates.
Inflation leaving out volatile items such as energy and food.

levels.headline: Markets price in a Bank of England rate rise to 4% on 5 November after inflation hits 3.5%
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, above the 3.4% consensus and the highest since October 2025. Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier, and the energy shock is linked to the US-Iran conflict and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
Core inflation rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, and services inflation accelerated to 3.7%. Bank Rate stands at 3.75% after the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold it in September, with three members wanting a rise.
Markets now price a 98% chance of a 25 basis point rise to 4% at the next meeting on 5 November. The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: Higher rates make mortgages and loans dearer, though they can help savers.

levels.headline: A Bank of England rate rise looks almost certain next week as inflation climbs
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% expected. It is the highest rate since October 2025. Fuel was the main driver, with motor fuel up 29.8% on the year, linked to the conflict involving Iran and problems in the Strait of Hormuz.
Core inflation, which strips out energy and food, rose to 2.8%, and services inflation was 3.7%. In September the Bank's rate-setters voted 6-3 to keep Bank Rate at 3.75%, with three wanting a rise.
Markets see a 98% chance the Bank raises it by a quarter of a point to 4% on 5 November.
levels.why: It affects borrowing costs for households and businesses.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.5%, and a Bank of England interest rate rise is expected on 5 November
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, up from 3.1% in August. That was more than the 3.4% economists expected, and it is the highest figure for nearly a year. Petrol and diesel were nearly 30% dearer, which is linked to the war involving Iran and disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Prices excluding energy and food rose 2.8%, and prices of services rose 3.7%. The Bank of England's rate-setting committee voted 6-3 in September to keep its rate at 3.75%.
Investors now think there is a 98% chance the rate goes up to 4% on 5 November.
levels.why: If the rate rises, mortgages and loans could cost more.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise rates after inflation rises to 3.5%
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% that economists expected. Fuel was the main cause, with petrol and diesel almost 30% dearer than a year ago after the war involving Iran disrupted oil supplies.
The Bank of England's main interest rate is 3.75%. At its last meeting in September, six members of its rate-setting committee voted to hold it and three voted to raise it. Investors now think there is a 98% chance that it will go up by a quarter of a point to 4% on 5 November.
A higher rate makes borrowing dearer for people with variable-rate mortgages or loans, though savers may earn more.
levels.why: It affects the cost of mortgages, loans and savings.

levels.headline: UK prices are rising faster, so the Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates
levels.body:
Prices in the UK rose by 3.5% over the year to September, up from 3.1% the month before. Experts had expected 3.4%. It is the fastest rise for almost a year. Fuel cost nearly 30% more than a year ago, which is linked to the war involving Iran and trouble shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Prices of things other than energy and food rose 2.8%, and prices of services, such as haircuts and train tickets, rose 3.7%.
The Bank of England sets the main interest rate, which is now 3.75%. Last time, six members voted to keep it and three wanted a rise. Investors now think a rise to 4% on 5 November is almost certain.
levels.why: Interest rates affect what people pay on loans and earn on savings.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster in the UK, so interest rates are expected to go up
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year before. In August the figure was 3.1%. Experts had guessed 3.4%. This rise in prices is called inflation, and it is now at its highest for almost a year. Petrol and diesel cost nearly 30% more, because of a war involving Iran and problems moving oil by sea.
The Bank of England is the bank that looks after the country's money. It sets the main interest rate, which is 3.75% now. In September, six of its nine rate-setters voted to keep it. Three wanted it higher.
Investors think the rate will almost certainly go up to 4% on 5 November. That would make borrowing dearer.
levels.why: A higher rate can make mortgages dearer but help savers.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, so borrowing money may get dearer
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier. The figure was 3.1% in August. When prices keep rising like this, it is called inflation. It means your money buys a little less than before. Petrol and diesel were the main cause. They cost nearly 30% more, because of a war involving Iran that makes oil harder to ship.
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. It sets an interest rate, which is the price of borrowing. The rate is now 3.75%. Three of its nine rate-setters wanted it higher last time.
People who trade money think the Bank will raise the rate to 4% on 5 November. That is almost certain.
levels.why: It changes what families pay on loans and what they earn from savings.

levels.headline: Prices are rising more quickly, and the cost of borrowing may go up
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are rising faster. In September they were 3.5% higher than a year before. In August it was 3.1%. This is called inflation. It means a pound buys a bit less each year. The main cause is fuel. Petrol and diesel cost nearly 30% more than last year, because a war is making it hard to ship oil.
The Bank of England is in charge of keeping prices steady. It sets the interest rate. This is the extra money you pay back when you borrow, or get paid when you save. The rate is 3.75% now. People who study money think it will go up to 4% on 5 November.
That would make loans a bit more costly.
levels.why: Your family might pay more on loans, but earn more on savings.

levels.headline: Things in shops cost more, so the bank that sets borrowing costs may act
levels.body:
Things in the UK cost more than they did a year ago. In September, prices were 3.5% higher. That is more than the month before. Grown-ups call this inflation. It is like finding that your pocket money buys fewer sweets than last year. Petrol and diesel are the main reason. They cost nearly 30% more, because a war far away makes oil hard to ship.
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. It sets the cost of borrowing, called the interest rate. If you borrow money, you pay a little extra back. That extra is interest. The rate is 3.75% now. People think it will go up to 4% on 5 November.
levels.why: It can change the cost of loans for families.

levels.headline: Things cost more, so the Bank might ask for more when lending
levels.body:
Things in shops cost more than they did last year. Imagine your favourite sweet cost 100p last year, and now it costs 103 or 104p. That kind of price rise is called inflation. Petrol and diesel went up the most. They cost nearly 30% more, because there is a war far away that makes it hard to move oil.
The Bank of England is like the bank for the whole country. It decides how much extra people pay when they borrow money. This extra is called interest. If you lend a friend a pound, you might ask for a little extra back. People think the Bank will ask for a bit more soon, on 5 November.
levels.why: It can change how much families pay when they borrow.

headline: Federal Reserve expected to hold rates this week, with a December hike now widely anticipated

terms.meaning: The Fed's main interest rate, which influences borrowing costs across the US.
The Fed's preferred measure of US inflation.
A vote against the majority decision.

levels.headline: Federal Reserve expected to hold rates this week, with a December hike now widely anticipated
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve meets on 27 and 28 October and is widely expected to keep its target range for the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4%. Futures pricing puts the chance of a hold at around 90%, and 93% of 30 economists and fund managers surveyed by CNBC expect a pause.
Looking further ahead, 76% of respondents expect a rise at the December meeting, and futures imply about a 78% probability. Minutes of the last meeting said most participants judged another increase would likely be appropriate by year end.
Inflation is the concern: the Fed's preferred PCE gauge showed core inflation at 3% and headline at 3.4% for August. At least two voters are expected to dissent, and Chair Kevin Warsh has rejected traditional forward guidance.
levels.why: US rates influence global borrowing costs, share prices and the dollar.

levels.headline: The Fed is set to pause this week, but economists expect a rise in December
levels.body:
Markets and economists broadly expect the Federal Reserve to leave rates alone at its 27 to 28 October meeting, keeping the target range at 3.75% to 4%. Futures give a hold roughly a 90% chance, while 93% of those in a CNBC survey expect a pause.
Most of the same group, 76%, expect an increase in December, and futures show a 78% chance. Minutes from the previous meeting indicated another rise would likely be right by the end of the year.
The worry is inflation, with the Fed's favoured measure at 3% for core prices and 3.4% overall in August. Some dissent is expected, and Chair Kevin Warsh has rejected forward guidance, so a surprise cannot be ruled out.
levels.why: It shapes mortgage, loan and exchange rates well beyond the US.

levels.headline: US central bank expected to hold interest rates, then raise them in December
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve is meeting on 27 and 28 October. Most experts expect it to leave its main interest rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%. Market prices suggest a 90% chance of this, and 93% of people in a CNBC survey agree.
Most also think rates will go up when the Fed meets in December. The notes from its last meeting said another rise would probably be right before the end of the year.
The reason is rising prices. The Fed's preferred measure showed core inflation at 3% and overall inflation at 3.4% in August. A few members are expected to vote against the decision. The Fed's chair, Kevin Warsh, does not give hints about future moves.
levels.why: What the Fed does affects borrowing costs around the world.

levels.headline: Federal Reserve expected to hold rates this week but raise them in December
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve is meeting on 27 and 28 October and is expected to keep its main interest rate at between 3.75% and 4%. Futures markets give that about a 90% chance, and 93% of those in a CNBC survey agree.
Most expect a rise in December, with about 76% of survey respondents and 78% in futures pricing predicting one. Minutes from the last meeting said another increase would probably be appropriate by the end of the year.
The Fed is worried about inflation, which its preferred measure put at 3.4% in August. Two or more members are expected to dissent from a hold, and Chair Kevin Warsh does not give forward guidance.
levels.why: US rates affect borrowing costs and currencies around the world.

levels.headline: The US central bank is expected to pause this week, but raise rates later this year
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, meets on 27 and 28 October. Most experts think it will keep its main interest rate unchanged at between 3.75% and 4%. Traders give this about a 90% chance, and 93% of those asked by CNBC agree.
Most also expect the Fed to raise rates in December. Notes from its last meeting said another rise would probably be needed by the end of the year.
The reason is prices, which are rising too fast. The Fed's favourite measure showed 3% for core prices and 3.4% overall in August. A couple of members are expected to disagree with the decision. The chair, Kevin Warsh, does not like to give hints about what comes next.
levels.why: US interest rates affect prices and borrowing in many other countries.

levels.headline: America's central bank will probably wait this week, then raise rates in December
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is America's central bank. It sets the main interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. This week it holds a two-day meeting, on 27 and 28 October. Most experts think it will leave the rate where it is, between 3.75% and 4%. Traders say there is about a 90% chance of that.
Most experts also think the Fed will raise the rate in December. Notes from its last meeting said another rise would probably be needed this year.
The reason is rising prices. In August they were rising by 3.4% over a year, a bit too fast. A few of the Fed's voters may disagree with the decision. Its chair is Kevin Warsh.
levels.why: A higher US rate can make borrowing dearer in other countries too.

levels.headline: The US bank that sets interest rates is likely to wait, then raise them in December
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. It sets the main interest rate, which is the cost of borrowing money. It meets on 27 and 28 October. Most experts think it will leave the rate where it is, between 3.75% and 4%.
Most also expect the rate to go up in December. In the notes from its last meeting, the Fed said another rise would probably be right this year.
Prices are rising too fast, which is why. In August they were 3.4% higher than a year before. A few members might vote against the decision. The Fed's boss is called Kevin Warsh, and he does not like to say what he will do next.
levels.why: The cost of borrowing in America affects prices around the world.

levels.headline: America's money bank will probably wait, but may raise its price for borrowing later
levels.body:
America has a money bank for the whole country. It is called the Federal Reserve. It decides the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It is having a meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday. Most experts think it will leave the rate where it is.
Most experts also think the rate will go up in December. A raise means borrowing costs more. The Fed does this when prices rise too fast. In August, prices were 3.4% higher than a year before. That is quicker than the Fed would like.
A few people at the Fed may not agree with the choice. Its boss is Kevin Warsh. He does not like to tell people his plans in advance.
levels.why: Rates in America can change what things cost far away.

levels.why: People who lead should be fair and kind to everybody.

headline: Home Secretary orders independent review of security for people in public life after terrorism charges

terms.meaning: Work to stop and investigate terrorist attacks.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
A law covering spying and foreign interference.

levels.headline: Home Secretary orders independent review of security for people in public life after terrorism charges
levels.body:
The Home Secretary has announced an independent review of the protective security the state gives people in public life, led by Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the former national security adviser. It will cover physical threats, online risks and dangers in a more polarised society, and report within six months. It complements Sir Robert Buckland's ongoing review into the killing of Sir David Amess.
On 2 October a suspect was charged with a terrorism offence, including preparing an act of terror against the leader of Reform UK. Separately, the government says the RAF Fairford incident was highly likely coordinated by a known individual in Iran and almost certainly directed by the IRGC.
Police have charged two men, Abdulkarim and Nouman Essghir, under the National Security Act 2023. Iran denies involvement.
levels.why: It could change how politicians and others in public life are protected from threats.

levels.headline: A six-month independent review will examine how the state protects people in public life

The Home Secretary has launched an independent review of protective security for people in public life. Sir Stephen Lovegrove, a former national security adviser, will lead it and report within six months. It will look at physical threats, online risks and the dangers of a polarised society, and sits alongside Sir Robert Buckland's review into the killing of Sir David Amess.

levels.why: It will shape protection for MPs and other public figures.

levels.headline: The UK orders a review of security for people in public life
levels.body:
The Home Secretary has ordered an independent review of the protection the state gives people in public life. It will be led by Sir Stephen Lovegrove, a former national security adviser. It will look at physical threats, dangers online and the risks of a more divided society. It must report within six months.

levels.headline: A new review will look at keeping politicians and public figures safe
levels.body:
The Home Secretary has started an independent review of how the government protects people in public life, such as politicians. levels.why: People who serve the public need to be safe.

levels.headline: The government orders a big check on how public figures are kept safe
levels.body:
The Home Secretary has ordered a big independent check on how the state keeps people in public life safe. This includes politicians. Sir Stephen Lovegrove, who used to advise the government on security, will lead it. He will look at physical dangers, dangers online and the risks in a country where people disagree strongly. On 2 October, a person was charged with a terrorism offence, including planning an attack on the leader of Reform UK. The government also says an incident at the RAF Fairford air base was very likely arranged by someone in Iran. Two men have been charged under a spying law. Iran says it was not involved.
levels.why: Keeping public figures safe helps keep democracy working.

levels.headline: A review will ask how well politicians and other public figures are protected
levels.body:
The Home Secretary is the minister in charge of police and security. The Home Secretary has ordered a review of how well people in public life are kept safe. This includes politicians. Sir Stephen Lovegrove, who used to give the government advice on security, will lead it. He will look at dangers in person and online. He has six months to report.
On 2 October, someone was charged with a terrorism offence, including planning an attack on the leader of Reform UK. Iran says it had nothing to do with it.
levels.why: Keeping public figures safe helps keep democracy strong.

levels.headline: The UK will check how well it keeps leaders and politicians safe
levels.body:
The Home Secretary is the minister in charge of police and security in the UK. The Home Secretary has asked an expert, Sir Stephen Lovegrove, to check how well politicians and other well-known people are kept safe. He will look at dangers in real life and online. He has six months to tell the government what he finds.
This comes after police charged someone on 2 October with a terrorism offence. The person is accused of planning an attack on the leader of a political party. The government also says an air base called RAF Fairford was targeted, and thinks someone in Iran was behind it. Iran says it was not.
levels.why: Leaders should be able to do their jobs without fear.

levels.headline: Experts will check how to keep important people safe
levels.body:
The Home Secretary is the minister who looks after the police and keeping people safe. The Home Secretary has asked an expert to check how well politicians and other well-known people are protected. Politicians are people we vote for to help run the country. The expert will look at dangers in the street and online. He has six months to tell the government what he finds.
This comes after police charged someone with planning an attack on a political leader. The government also thinks an air base was targeted, and that someone in another country, Iran, was behind it. Iran says it was not. Two men have been charged, and the courts will decide what happened.
levels.why: Everyone should be able to do their job without being afraid.

levels.headline: Some grown-ups will check that leaders are kept safe
levels.body:
The people who help run our country need to be kept safe, just as a school keeps teachers and pupils safe. The Home Secretary is the grown-up in charge of the police. The Home Secretary has asked an expert to check how well the country keeps well-known people safe. They include politicians, who are people we vote for. The expert has six months to tell the government what he finds.
This happened because police say someone planned to hurt a political leader. The police have caught the person. Police have also charged two men over an air base. The courts, not the government, will decide what is true.
levels.why: Everybody should be safe when they do their job.

headline: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine-US-Russia talks for November as Russian strikes continue

terms.meaning: Negotiations involving three parties; here Ukraine, Russia and the United States.
An agreement to stop fighting, for a time or in a place.
A person sent to represent their government.

levels.headline: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine-US-Russia talks for November as Russian strikes continue
levels.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 25 October that a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, the US and Russia will take place in November in an attempt to restart stalled peace talks. He said the agenda could cover territorial questions at leader level and other issues in technical groups.
Reports differ on when Moscow will return: one says after 10 November, another after 4 November, and the Kremlin has signalled mid-November, after the US midterms. US envoy Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, and Donald Trump said the sides were maybe now the closest they had been to ending the war.
Russian strikes continued, and a local ceasefire in Oleshky began on Tuesday. Euronews reports positions have barely shifted.
levels.why: The talks could shape the future of the war and Europe's security.

levels.headline: A new round of three-way peace talks is planned for November
levels.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 25 October that Ukraine, the US and Russia will hold a trilateral meeting in November to try to restart stalled peace efforts. He said territorial questions could be handled at leader level, with other matters in technical groups.
The date is unclear. Reports give after 4 November or after 10 November, and the Kremlin has suggested mid-November, after the US midterm elections. US envoy Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg, and Trump said the sides were perhaps the closest they had been to ending the conflict.
Russian attacks went on, and a local ceasefire in Oleshky began on Tuesday. Earlier talks produced little beyond prisoner exchanges.
levels.why: A deal could end the biggest war in Europe for decades.

levels.headline: Ukraine says peace talks with Russia and the US will restart in November
levels.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine said on 25 October that Ukraine, Russia and the United States will meet in November to try to restart peace talks that have stalled. He said that leaders could discuss land, while experts handle other issues.
Nobody has said exactly when. Some reports say after 4 November and others after 10 November. The Kremlin has hinted at mid-November, after the US midterm elections. A US envoy, Witkoff, met Russian President Vladimir Putin. Donald Trump said the two sides were maybe the closest they had been to ending the war.
Russia kept attacking. A local ceasefire began in the town of Oleshky on Tuesday.
levels.why: It shows whether the war could move closer to an end.

levels.headline: Ukraine says three-way talks with Russia and the US will take place in November
levels.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 25 October that Ukraine, Russia and the United States will hold a trilateral meeting in November to try to restart stalled peace talks. Leaders could discuss territory, while technical groups handle other issues.
The date is not settled. Some reports say after 4 November, others after 10 November, and the Kremlin has hinted at mid-November, after the US midterm elections. US envoy Witkoff met President Putin in St Petersburg, and President Trump said the sides were perhaps the closest they had been to ending the war.
Russian strikes continued, and a local ceasefire began in Oleshky.
levels.why: Peace talks could decide whether the war moves closer to an end.

levels.headline: Talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US are planned for November
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on 25 October that there will be a three-way meeting in November. The sides are Ukraine, Russia and the United States. They want to restart peace talks that have stopped. He said that leaders could talk about land, while experts handle smaller matters.
The exact date is not clear. Some reports say after 4 November, others after 10 November. Russia has hinted at mid-November, after elections in the US. A US envoy met Russia's president, Vladimir Putin. President Trump said the two sides might be the closest they had been to ending the war.
Russia kept attacking Ukraine. A small local ceasefire began in the town of Oleshky.
levels.why: A deal could end a war that has hurt millions of people.

levels.headline: Ukraine, Russia and the US plan to talk about ending the war
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said that Ukraine, Russia and the United States will meet in November. They will try to restart talks about ending the war, which stopped for a while. He said leaders might talk about land. Experts might talk about smaller matters.
The date is not fixed. Russia has hinted at mid-November, after elections in the US. An envoy from the US, which means a person sent to speak for their country, met Russia's president, Vladimir Putin. US president Donald Trump said both sides may be the closest they have been to ending the war.
But Russia kept attacking. Earlier talks did not achieve much, apart from swapping prisoners.
levels.why: Peace would end the suffering of people in Ukraine.

levels.headline: Three countries plan to talk about ending the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine, and the war has gone on for a long time. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says Ukraine, Russia and the United States will meet in November. They want to talk about how to stop the war. Talks stopped for a while.
Nobody has said the exact day. Russia has hinted at the middle of November. A person from the US went to meet Russia's president, Vladimir Putin. The US president, Donald Trump, said both sides may be the closest they have been to ending the war.
But Russia is still attacking. Earlier talks did not achieve much, apart from the swapping of prisoners.
levels.why: Peace would help the people living there.

levels.headline: Leaders plan to talk about how to stop the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
There is a war in Ukraine, a country in Europe. Russia is attacking it. Many people have been hurt, and many have lost their homes. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says leaders from Ukraine, Russia and the United States will meet in November to try to talk about peace. Talks stopped for a while.
Nobody knows the exact day yet. Russia has hinted at the middle of November. A person from the US has already met Russia's president, Vladimir Putin. The American president, Donald Trump, said they may be the closest they have been to ending the war.
But the attacks have not stopped. Earlier talks did not achieve much.
levels.why: If the leaders agree, people could be safe again.

levels.headline: Three leaders plan to talk about ending a war
levels.body:
There is a war in a country called Ukraine. Another country, Russia, is attacking it. Many people have been hurt, and many have had to leave their homes. The leader of Ukraine says that people from Ukraine, Russia and America will meet next month to try to talk about peace.
It is like when two children fall out and a teacher gets them to sit down and talk. Nobody knows the exact day yet. The talks might be in the middle of November. The leaders have tried before, but it did not work.
The fighting has not stopped while they plan.
levels.why: If they agree, people could be safe again.

levels.headline: Grown-ups plan to talk about stopping a war
levels.body:
There is a war in a faraway country called Ukraine. Another country, Russia, is attacking it. Many people have been hurt. Many families have had to leave their homes.
The leader of Ukraine says that people from Ukraine, Russia and America will meet next month to talk about peace. It is like when two children fall out and a teacher asks them to sit down and talk it through. The teacher cannot make them be friends, but it can help.
Nobody knows the exact day yet. They have tried before, and it did not work. The fighting has not stopped while they plan.
levels.why: If they agree, families could be safe again.

headline: Eurozone inflation hits a three-year high of 3.8% as energy prices surge

terms.meaning: The group of European countries that use the euro as their currency.
Inflation excluding volatile items such as energy and food.
The ECB's key interest rate paid on banks' deposits.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation hits a three-year high of 3.8% as energy prices surge
levels.body:
Eurozone inflation rose to 3.8% in September, the highest in three years, with energy prices up 18.9% on the year. Core inflation was milder, edging up to 2.5% from 2.4%. Lithuania had the highest rate at 6.1% and Malta the lowest at 2.4%.
The European Central Bank raised its key rate to 2.5% on 10 September, its second rise this year. Its projections see inflation averaging 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, and it upgraded growth forecasts to 0.9% for 2026 and 1.4% for 2027.
Traders expect the ECB to hold on 29 October and raise again in December, though sources differ on the October outcome. The euro has also fallen to lows against the dollar not seen since May last year.
levels.why: Higher euro-area prices and rates affect UK exports, holidays and the wider economy.

levels.headline: Energy costs push euro-area inflation to its highest in three years
levels.body:
Inflation across the euro area reached 3.8% in September, a three-year high, with energy prices 18.9% higher than a year earlier. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, was 2.5%, up from 2.4%. Lithuania recorded 6.1%, Malta 2.4%.
The ECB lifted its key interest rate to 2.5% on 10 September, its second rise this year. It expects inflation to average 3.0% this year, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, and now forecasts growth of 0.9% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027.
Markets expect no change at the 29 October meeting and a rise in December, though sources disagree. The euro has slipped to its weakest against the dollar since May last year.
levels.why: It shows the energy shock reaching across Europe and affecting borrowing costs.

levels.headline: Prices across the euro area are rising at their fastest for three years
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro were 3.8% higher in September than a year before. That is the fastest rise in three years. Energy was 18.9% dearer. Prices excluding energy and food rose by 2.5%. Lithuania had the highest rate, at 6.1%, and Malta the lowest, at 2.4%.
The European Central Bank raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on 10 September. It was the second rise this year. The bank expects inflation to average 3.0% this year. It also expects the economy to grow by 0.9%.
Traders think the bank will wait on 29 October and raise rates again in December. The euro has also fallen against the dollar.
levels.why: Higher prices and rates in Europe can affect trade, holidays and the UK economy.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation reaches 3.8%, highest in three years
levels.body:
Inflation across the countries that use the euro reached 3.8% in September, the highest in three years. Energy was 18.9% more expensive than a year earlier. Prices excluding energy and food rose by 2.5%. Lithuania had the highest rate at 6.1% and Malta the lowest at 2.4%.
The European Central Bank raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on 10 September, its second rise this year. It expects inflation to average 3.0% in 2026 and growth of 0.9%.
Traders expect it to hold rates on 29 October and raise them again in December, though sources differ. The euro has also fallen to its lowest against the dollar since May last year.
levels.why: Higher prices and rates in Europe can affect UK trade and holidays.

levels.headline: Prices in countries that use the euro are rising fastest in three years
levels.body:
Prices in the 20-odd countries that use the euro were 3.8% higher in September than a year before. That is the biggest rise in three years. Energy was 18.9% more expensive. Prices without energy and food rose by 2.5%. In Lithuania prices rose 6.1%, the most, and in Malta 2.4%, the least.
The European Central Bank sets interest rates for those countries. On 10 September it raised its main rate to 2.5%, for the second time this year. It expects growth of 0.9% this year.
Traders think the bank will leave rates alone on 29 October and raise them in December. The euro has also lost value against the dollar.
levels.why: Europe is a big trading partner, so what happens there can reach the UK.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster in the countries that use the euro
levels.body:
Prices in countries that use the euro, such as France and Germany, were 3.8% higher in September than a year before. This is the fastest rise for three years. It is called inflation. Energy cost 18.9% more, because of the war in the Middle East. Prices of other things rose more slowly, by 2.5%. Lithuania saw 6.1% and Malta only 2.4%.
The European Central Bank sets interest rates for the euro. It raised the rate to 2.5% on 10 September. People who watch money think it will wait on 29 October, then raise the rate in December. The euro has also lost value against the dollar.
levels.why: It can make holidays in Europe and trade with Europe cost more.

levels.headline: Shop prices are going up faster in countries that use the euro
levels.body:
Prices in countries that use the euro, such as France and Germany, were 3.8% higher in September than a year before. That is the fastest rise in three years. The main cause is energy, which cost 18.9% more. Other prices went up more slowly, by 2.5%. Some countries have it worse than others. Prices rose 6.1% in Lithuania and only 2.4% in Malta.
The European Central Bank decides interest rates for those countries. It raised its rate to 2.5% in September. People who follow money think it will wait this week, then raise it again in December. The euro has become worth less compared with the dollar.
levels.why: Many families in Europe are paying more for everyday things.

levels.headline: Things cost more in many European countries
levels.body:
Many European countries share the euro as their money. Prices there went up faster this year. In September, things cost 3.8% more than a year before. This is the fastest rise in three years. Energy, such as petrol and gas, cost 18.9% more. Some places had it worse. Prices in Lithuania rose 6.1%, but in Malta only 2.4%.
A bank called the European Central Bank decides the price of borrowing for all these countries. In September it raised that price to 2.5%. People think it will raise it again in December. The euro has also become worth a bit less than the dollar.
levels.why: Families in Europe are paying more, and this can reach us too.

levels.headline: Things in shops cost more in countries that share the euro
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe share the same money, called the euro. This year, shop prices there have gone up faster. In September, things cost 3.8% more than a year ago. It is like a sweet that cost 100 cents now costing 104. Energy, such as petrol and gas, went up the most.
A bank called the European Central Bank looks after the euro for all these countries. It can make borrowing cost more, to slow price rises. It did this in September. People think it will do it again in December.
Some places have it worse. In one country, Lithuania, things cost 6.1% more.
levels.why: Families there have less money to spend on other things.

levels.headline: Prices are going up in lots of European countries
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe share one kind of money, called the euro. Prices there have gone up this year. A sweet that cost 100 cents last year may now cost 104. Petrol and gas went up the most, because there is a war in the Middle East.
There is a bank for all these countries. It is called the European Central Bank. When prices go up too fast, it can make borrowing cost more. People then spend a bit less, and prices can stop rising so fast. The bank did this in September. People think it might do it again before Christmas.
Some families have it harder than others. They have less money left for fun things.
levels.why: Families have less money for other things.

headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.7% in a surprise move, ONS says

terms.meaning: The share of people who are looking for work and available to start, out of everyone working or looking.
Not working and not looking for work, for example students or people who are long-term sick.
People paid through the tax system by an employer.

levels.headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.7% in a surprise move, ONS says
levels.body:
The ONS reported on 20 October that the UK unemployment rate fell by 0.1 percentage points on both the quarter and the year to 4.7% in the three months to August 2026, about 1.71 million people. Trading Economics said markets had expected it to stay at 4.9%.
The employment rate for those aged 16 to 64 rose 0.2 points to 75.3%, and economic inactivity fell by 0.2 points on the year to 20.9%. There were 2.4 unemployed people per vacancy, down from 2.5.
The ONS describes the labour market as broadly flat in 2026, and the number of payrolled employees has fallen over the same period. The next labour market release is due on 17 November.
levels.why: Jobs data guides interest rates and shows how secure work feels.

levels.headline: A surprise fall in unemployment, though the jobs market remains flat
levels.body:
Unemployment in the UK fell to 4.7% in June to August 2026, down 0.1 points on both the quarter and the year, according to the ONS. That is about 1.71 million people. Markets had expected it to stay at 4.9%.
The employment rate for 16 to 64 year olds rose to 75.3%, and inactivity fell to 20.9%. There were 2.4 unemployed people for every vacancy, compared with 2.5 earlier.
The ONS says the labour market has been broadly flat this year and the number of payrolled employees has fallen. The next release is on 17 November.
levels.why: It affects wages, spending and the Bank of England's choices.

levels.headline: UK unemployment drops unexpectedly to 4.7%
levels.body:
Official figures show that UK unemployment fell to 4.7% in the three months to August. That is 0.1 points lower than both the previous three months and a year earlier, and about 1.71 million people. Experts had expected it to stay at 4.9%.
More people are in work: 75.3% of those aged 16 to 64, up 0.2 points. The share not working and not looking for work fell to 20.9%. There were 2.4 unemployed people for each job vacancy, down from 2.5.
The Office for National Statistics says the jobs market has been broadly flat this year, and fewer people are on company payrolls. New figures are due on 17 November.
levels.why: It shows whether jobs are easy or hard to find.

levels.headline: UK unemployment falls unexpectedly to 4.7%
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, according to the Office for National Statistics. That is down 0.1 percentage points on both the previous quarter and the year before, and means about 1.71 million people. Economists had expected 4.9%.
The employment rate for people aged 16 to 64 rose to 75.3%. The share of people neither working nor looking for work fell to 20.9%. There were 2.4 unemployed people for every vacancy, down from 2.5.
The ONS says the jobs market has been broadly flat in 2026 and that the number of payrolled employees has fallen. The next figures are due on 17 November.
levels.why: It shows how easy or hard it is to find work, and it influences interest rates.

levels.headline: The number of people out of work in the UK has fallen a little
levels.body:
Official figures say 4.7% of people in the UK who wanted a job did not have one in the three months to August. That is about 1.71 million people. It is 0.1 points lower than before, and it surprised experts, who had expected 4.9%.
More people have jobs now. About 75.3% of people aged 16 to 64 are in work. The number of people who are not working and not looking for work fell too, to 20.9%. There were 2.4 jobless people for every job opening, down from 2.5.
The Office for National Statistics says the jobs market has been steady this year. New figures come out on 17 November.
levels.why: A strong jobs market helps families, but it can also push up prices.

levels.headline: Fewer people in the UK are out of work than expected
levels.body:
New official figures say 4.7% of people in the UK who want a job do not have one. That is about 1.71 million people. It is a little lower than before, and lower than experts expected. They had guessed 4.9%.
More people are working now. Around 75 in every 100 people aged 16 to 64 have a job. Fewer people are neither working nor looking for work. For every job opening there are 2.4 people looking for one, a little fewer than before.
The Office for National Statistics counts these numbers. It says the jobs market has been fairly steady this year. New figures come out on 17 November.
levels.why: It tells us how easy it is to find a job.

levels.headline: A few more people in the UK have jobs than before
levels.body:
The government counts how many people want a job and cannot find one. The latest count says 4.7% of people in the UK are in that group. That is about 1.7 million people. It is a bit lower than the last count, and experts were surprised. They thought it would be 4.9%.
About 75 out of every 100 people aged 16 to 64 now have a job. For each job that is advertised, there are 2.4 people looking for work. That is slightly fewer than before.
The Office for National Statistics counts these numbers. It says the jobs market has been fairly steady this year.
levels.why: Jobs help families to pay for the things they need.

levels.headline: Slightly fewer grown-ups in the UK are looking for work
levels.body:
Every few weeks, the government counts how many grown-ups want a job but do not have one. This time, 4.7 in every 100 people were in that group. That is a bit fewer than last time. Experts had expected a few more.
About 75 in every 100 people aged 16 to 64 have jobs. Sometimes more people look for the same job. There are 2.4 people looking for each job that is advertised. That used to be 2.5, so it is slightly easier to find work.
The numbers come from a team called the Office for National Statistics. It says the jobs market has been fairly steady this year.
levels.why: Jobs mean families can pay for food, homes and fun.

levels.headline: Fewer grown-ups are looking for jobs than before
levels.body:
Some grown-ups want a job but cannot find one. The government counts them. This time, about 5 in every 100 of them did not have a job. That is a bit fewer than last time. Most grown-ups aged 16 to 64 had jobs. That was about 75 in every 100.
Imagine a school shop that needs helpers. If lots of people want to help but there are only a few places, some will miss out. In the UK right now, for each job advertised, about two or three people want it. That is slightly fewer than before.
The team that counts is called the Office for National Statistics.
levels.why: Jobs let families buy food, pay for homes and enjoy fun things.

levels.headline: Slightly more grown-ups have jobs than before
levels.body:
Grown-ups often go to work to earn money. Money pays for food, homes and fun things. Some grown-ups want a job but cannot find one yet. The government counts how many. This time, the number went down a little. That is good news for those families.
Imagine a school shop that needs helpers. If lots of people want to help but there are only a few places, some will miss out. In the UK right now, for each job, about two or three people want it. That is slightly fewer people than before, so each person has a slightly better chance.
levels.why: Jobs help families pay for the things they need.

headline: Energy price cap rises 4% to £1,723 a year, with a VAT cut on electricity softening the blow

terms.meaning: A limit on the most suppliers can charge per unit of energy on standard tariffs.
Value Added Tax, a sales tax added to many goods and services.
An energy deal with a set price for a period.

levels.headline: Energy price cap rises 4% to £1,723 a year, with a VAT cut on electricity softening the blow
levels.body:
Ofgem raised the energy price cap by 4%, from £1,663 to £1,723 a year for a typical household, covering 1 October to 31 December 2026. The cap limits what suppliers can charge on standard variable tariffs.
VAT on household electricity was cut from 5% to zero from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, while gas stays at 5%. Ofgem says the cut kept the cap about £45 lower than it otherwise would have been. levels.headline: Gas and electricity cost a bit more now
levels.body:
Gas and electricity keep our homes warm and lit. This autumn they cost a little more. A rule says the most that energy companies can charge. This rule is called the price cap. A typical home now pays about £1,723 for the year. Last time it was £1,663. That is about 4% more.
The government has also cut a tax on electricity. A tax is money everyone pays to the government. Without the cut, electricity would cost about £45 more. The cut lasts until March next year. Some families have a fixed deal, which means their price is set and does not change.
It is not clear what will happen after March.
levels.why: Heating and lights are costs families need to pay.

levels.headline: Keeping warm costs a little more this winter
levels.body:
Gas and electricity keep our homes warm and bright. This autumn, they cost a little more. There is a rule that says the most a company can charge. A typical home now pays about £1,723 for the year. A little while ago it was £1,663. That is a small rise, like a sweet going up a few pence.
The government cut a tax on electricity, so it did not go up even more. A tax is money that everyone pays to the government. The cut lasts until March next year. Some families have a fixed deal, so their price stays the same for a while.
Nobody knows what will happen after March.
levels.why: Warm homes matter to families, so prices matter too.
